findings.message: `_convert_resp_floats` blindly calls `float()` on every string leaf of a JSON.RESP reply, so any *string* value or object key whose text happens to parse as a number is silently converted. `{"a": "3.14"}` now yields `3.14` (float) instead of the string, `{"1": ...}` turns the key into `1.0`, and string values like `"inf"`/`"nan"`/`"1e5"` become floats. This both corrupts user data and re-introduces a RESP2/RESP3 divergence (RESP3 keeps those as strings, since only real JSON numbers arrive as doubles). The conversion needs to be restricted to leaves that cannot be JSON strings (e.g. by tracking the `"{"`/`"["` structure markers) rather than "anything that parses as a float".

`TSInfo.__init__` takes the RESP3 dict as-is (`response = args`) without decoding keys. With `protocol=3` and the default `decode_responses=False` the map keys are bytes (`b"totalSamples"`, `b"labels"`, ...), so every `response.get("...")` returns `None` and the returned `TSInfo` has all-`None` attributes and `labels == {}`. Since this diff moves `INFO_CMD: TSInfo` into the shared `_MODULE_CALLBACKS`, RESP3 users now get silently empty info objects where they previously got the raw dict. Decode the keys the same way `redis/commands/bf/info.py::_parse_info_args` does (`{nativestr(k): v ...}`).

`_normalize_info_attribute` classifies attribute tokens using the fixed whitelist `_INFO_ATTR_PAIR_KEYS = {identifier, attribute, type, WEIGHT, SEPARATOR, PHONETIC}`. Any other key/value pair emitted by FT.INFO is flattened into `flags`: for a VECTOR field the RESP2 output becomes `{"identifier":..., "type":"VECTOR", "flags":["algorithm","FLAT","data_type","FLOAT32","dim",128,"distance_metric","COSINE"]}` (note the non-string `128` from `str_if_bytes(int)`), while `_parse_info_resp3` returns them as real dict keys. So FT.INFO is still protocol-divergent and the RESP2 shape loses structure for vector/geoshape/newer field types. Consider deriving pairs positionally (value follows key unless the token is a known flag) or keeping the unknown tokens as pairs.

`AggregateResult` gains `total`/`warnings`, and `_parse_aggregate_resp3` populates `total` from `total_results`, but the RESP2 path (`_parse_aggregate`/`_get_aggregate_result`, unchanged in this diff) still calls `AggregateResult(rows, cursor, schema)`. Result: `ft().aggregate(...).total` is the real count under RESP3 and always `0` under RESP2 — the opposite of the unification goal, and contradicting docs/resp_unification.rst which documents `result.total == 5` for both protocols.

`_TDigestBloomBase._RESP3_MODULE_CALLBACKS` is still `{}`, so TDIGEST.BYRANK/BYREVRANK/CDF/QUANTILE keep the RESP2-only `parse_to_list` callback. Under RESP2 an integral result comes back as `int` (and `"inf"` stays a `str`), while RESP3 returns native doubles — the values are not unified, yet `redis/commands/bf/commands.py` now annotates these methods as returning `list[float]` and the added migration docs claim a RESP3 parser was added. Either register the RESP3 callback or fix the annotations/docs.

`Pipeline.__init__`/`AsyncPipeline.__init__` copy the callbacks with `dict(response_callbacks)`. The client stores them in a `CaseInsensitiveDict`; converting to a plain `dict` makes callback lookup in `parse_response` case-sensitive for this pipeline, so e.g. `pipe.execute_command("get", "foo")` (or any lower/mixed-case command name) silently loses its response callback. Use `CaseInsensitiveDict(response_callbacks)` (or `.copy()` preserving the type) instead.

Defining `client` as a property that returns `self` on the search `Pipeline`/`AsyncPipeline` shadows the inherited public `Redis.client()` method (as the AsyncPipeline docstring itself notes). `pipe.client()` now raises `TypeError: 'Pipeline' object is not callable` instead of returning a single-connection client. Prefer an internal attribute/helper (e.g. `_protocol_client`) and have `_parse_results` use it, rather than overriding a documented public method.

`parse_function_list(response)` is registered as a response callback but, unlike every other callback here, it does not accept `**options`. Response callbacks are invoked as `callback(response, **options)`; any option that ends up in the queued command's options (now or later, e.g. a cluster/pipeline internal kwarg) will raise `TypeError: parse_function_list() got an unexpected keyword argument`. Add `**options` for consistency and safety.

Dropping `decode_string_values=True` from `parse_memory_stats` does not unify MEMORY STATS: RESP2 sends the ratio/percentage fields (`allocator-frag-ratio`, `rss-overhead-ratio`, `peak.percentage`, ...) as bulk strings, so with `decode_responses=False` those values now come back as `bytes` (previously `str`) while RESP3 returns native floats. This is a regression for RESP2 users and still protocol-divergent, contrary to the documented "native int values" claim.

This PR commits ~1000 lines of internal AI planning artefacts (`.agent/resp2_vs_resp3_implementation_plan.md`, `.agent/resp2_vs_resp3_command_analysis.md`) plus `specs/resp2_resp3_migration_guide.md`, which duplicates the same command tables already added in `docs/resp_unification.rst` (and the specs file has no trailing newline). Three copies of the same migration matrix will drift; keep the user-facing guide under `docs/` only and drop the planning files from the repository.

`TSInfo.__init__` now accepts the RESP3 map directly (`response = args`) without normalising keys. Under RESP3 with `decode_responses=False` the server map has **bytes** keys (b"totalSamples", b"labels", ...), so every `response.get("...")` returns `None` and the resulting `TSInfo` has all attributes `None`/`{}`. Since `TS.INFO` was moved into the shared `_MODULE_CALLBACKS`, this now silently affects all RESP3 clients that do not decode responses. Compare with `redis/commands/bf/info.py::_parse_info_args`, which correctly does `{nativestr(k): v for k, v in args.items()}` — the same normalisation is needed here.

`_convert_resp_floats` coerces *any* string leaf that parses as a float into a Python float. The docstring's premise ("any string that parses as a float must be a JSON float") is wrong: JSON *string* values and JSON *object keys* are also sent as bulk strings in RESP2. So `JSON.RESP` on `{"10": "3.5"}` will turn both the key `"10"` and the string value `"3.5"` into floats, corrupting user data and re-introducing a RESP2/RESP3 divergence (RESP3 sends JSON strings as blobs and doubles as doubles, so they remain distinguishable there). `float("nan")`/`float("inf")` string values are affected too.

`AggregateResult` gains a new `total` attribute, but only `_parse_aggregate_resp3` populates it; the RESP2 parser (`_parse_aggregate`/`_get_aggregate_result`) still constructs `AggregateResult(rows, cursor, schema)`, leaving `total == 0`. A newly-advertised attribute that is always 0 on RESP2 is a trap and contradicts the unification goal (and the RESP3 doc table which advertises `result.total == 5`). Either populate it from the RESP2 reply's first element or don't expose it yet.

`Pipeline.__init__` registers response callbacks for the full union of module commands (INFO, CONFIG, SPELLCHECK, SYNDUMP included), implying they are now pipeline-safe. However only `search`, `aggregate`, `profile` and `hybrid_search` were given the `if isinstance(res, Pipeline): return res` guard. `SearchCommands.info()/config_get()/spellcheck()/syndump()` still call `self._parse_results(CMD, res)` on the returned Pipeline object, which raises (`TypeError: 'Pipeline' object is not iterable` / `AttributeError: 'Pipeline' has no attribute 'items'`) instead of queueing the command. Add the same guard to those four methods.

`_TDigestBloomBase` still leaves `_RESP3_MODULE_CALLBACKS = {}`, so `TDIGEST.BYRANK/BYREVRANK/CDF/QUANTILE` get `parse_to_list` on RESP2 only. RESP2 therefore yields the string `"inf"` for out-of-range ranks while RESP3 yields `float('inf')` — the very divergence this PR claims to fix, and `docs/resp_unification.rst` explicitly documents these commands as unified (`[0.5, "inf"]` on RESP3). Either add the RESP3 callbacks or correct the documentation.

`_parse_hybrid_search` now runs every value through `decode_field_value`, which falls back to `str_if_bytes` (utf-8, errors="replace") when no per-field encoding is registered. Previously FT.HYBRID values were returned as raw bytes on RESP2 (NEVER_DECODE is set). This is an undocumented breaking change (bytes -> str) and it lossily mangles binary payloads (e.g. vector fields pulled in via LOAD) unless the caller remembers to call the brand-new `HybridQuery.return_field(..., decode_field=False)`. It also ignores `decode_responses=False`. Worth documenting in the migration tables at minimum.

This PR ships ~1,000 lines of internal planning artifacts (`.agent/resp2_vs_resp3_command_analysis.md`, `.agent/resp2_vs_resp3_implementation_plan.md`, `specs/resp2_resp3_migration_guide.md`). The last one largely duplicates the new `docs/resp_unification.rst` and will drift out of sync; the `.agent/` files reference implementation state that is already inaccurate (e.g. TDigest RESP3 callbacks). Consider dropping them and keeping only `docs/resp_unification.rst`.

`protocol` is still typed `Optional[int]` and is forwarded verbatim into `connection_kwargs`, so an explicit `Redis(protocol=None)` leaves `connection_kwargs["protocol"] is None`. `dict.get("protocol", DEFAULT_RESP_VERSION)` returns `None` (the key exists), `check_protocol_version(None, 3)` is False, and the RESP2 callback table is installed — but `AbstractConnection.__init__` coerces `None` to `DEFAULT_RESP_VERSION` (now 3) and the connection actually speaks RESP3 with a RESP3 parser. Before this change both sides resolved to 2, so this is a new client/wire mismatch (responses parsed with the wrong callbacks). Use `connection_kwargs.get("protocol") or DEFAULT_RESP_VERSION` (or normalise `None` in `__init__`). The identical pattern was added in `redis/asyncio/client.py` (~line 414) and has the same problem.

`ConnectionPool.get_protocol()` (sync and async) still returns `connection_kwargs.get("protocol", None)`. Now that connections default to RESP3, a pool built directly (`ConnectionPool(host=...)`, no `protocol` kwarg) reports `None` while its connections negotiate RESP3; callers that branch on `get_protocol() in [3, "3"]` (e.g. PubSub health-check response shape) will take the RESP2 branch. Consider defaulting it to `DEFAULT_RESP_VERSION` alongside the other call sites updated in this diff.

`assert_kwargs_match` replaces exact-equality assertions with a subset check (`expected.items() <= actual.items()`), so the URL-parsing tests no longer detect *extra* or wrongly-injected kwargs (e.g. a spurious `port`, `db`, or duplicated option would now pass). Prefer stripping the known maint-notification keys from `actual` and asserting equality on the remainder, so the parsing behaviour stays fully pinned.

The new text says "RESP3 is the default protocol used by the client" but the example immediately below still passes `protocol=3`, and the sentence "To use support for RESP3, ensure you have at least version 5.0 of the client" no longer parses. Drop `protocol=3` from the snippet (or state the redis-py version from which it became the default, as the notebooks/rst do) so the README is self-consistent.
Stray whitespace-only edit: `    },` was re-indented to `     },` in the output cell, unrelated to the RESP3 documentation change. Revert to keep the notebook JSON indentation consistent.

`connection_kwargs.get("protocol", DEFAULT_RESP_VERSION)` only applies the default when the key is *absent*; an explicit `protocol=None` (allowed by the `Optional[int]` signature, and `Redis.__init__` always writes `"protocol": protocol` into `connection_kwargs`) still yields `None`. `check_protocol_version(None, 3)` is False, so RESP2 callbacks are installed, while `AbstractConnection.__init__` converts `None` to `DEFAULT_RESP_VERSION` (now 3) and negotiates `HELLO 3`. The result is a RESP3 connection parsed with RESP2 callbacks (e.g. `HGETALL` returns a map that is then fed to `pairs_to_dict`). Before this change both sides resolved to 2, so they agreed. Consider normalizing with `kwargs.get("protocol") or DEFAULT_RESP_VERSION` (same pattern repeated in redis/asyncio/client.py:414, redis/cluster.py, redis/asyncio/cluster.py, redis/connection.py).

Because the default protocol is now 3, `check_protocol_version(kwargs.get("protocol", DEFAULT_RESP_VERSION), 3)` is True for every pool that does not explicitly opt out, so a `MaintNotificationsConfig()` is auto-created and maintenance notifications become enabled by default. Two consequences: (1) for `UnixDomainSocketConnection` pools there is no `host`, so `_enable_maintenance_notifications()` hits `if host is None: raise ValueError(...)`; ValueError is not a `ResponseError`, so the `enabled == "auto"` escape hatch does not apply and the exception propagates out of `on_connect()` — unix-socket clients would fail to connect by default; (2) `connection_kwargs` now always gains `maint_notifications_pool_handler`, `maint_notifications_config`, `orig_host_address`, `orig_socket_timeout`, `orig_socket_connect_timeout`, which will raise `TypeError` for user-supplied `connection_class` implementations that do not accept these kwargs (the new `assert_kwargs_match` helper in tests confirms these keys are now always injected).

`ClientT = redis.Redis | redis.RedisCluster` is a module-level *runtime* expression (not an annotation), so PEP 604 `X | Y` on classes requires Python 3.10+. `from __future__ import annotations` does not help here. On Python 3.9 (still listed as supported: "redis-py 6.2.0 supports Python 3.9+") this raises `TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for |` at import time, which would fail collection of the entire async command test module, not just the new XNACK tests. Use `typing.Union[...]` or a string alias instead. (Also, in an asyncio test module the alias should reference `redis.asyncio.Redis`/`redis.asyncio.RedisCluster`.)

`test_xnack_invalid_mode`, `test_xnack_no_ids` and `test_xnack_negative_retrycount` (and their asyncio counterparts) only exercise client-side argument validation in `xnack()` — no server round-trip is required for the raise. Gating them behind `@skip_if_server_version_lt("8.7.2")` means the validation logic is never covered on any currently released Redis server, so a regression in the DataError checks would go unnoticed until 8.7.2 is in CI. Drop the version gate on the pure-validation tests.

XNACK targets an unreleased Redis version (tests gate on 8.7.2), i.e. it is a pre-GA server feature. Per the repo convention, unstable commands are marked with `@experimental_method()` from `redis.utils` (as done for `delex`, `digest`, `digest_local`) so users get a consistent warning; `xnack` is added without it.

Inconsistent token encoding in the argument list: `"IDS"` is a str while `b"RETRYCOUNT"` and `b"FORCE"` are bytes. Both encode fine, but pick one form (surrounding stream commands use plain str tokens) for readability.
`CLI` is inserted after `CMSCommands`, breaking the file's alphabetical ordering (should go between `CFCommands` and `CMSCommands`).

The skill instructs the agent to follow `.agent/instructions.md`, and `specs/redis_commands_guide.md` references `.agent/sync_async_type_hints_overload_guide.md`, but neither file is added by this PR. If they do not already exist in the repo these are dangling references that will silently degrade the documented workflow.

`ClientT = redis.Redis | redis.RedisCluster` is a module-level runtime expression, not an annotation, so PEP 604 union syntax is evaluated eagerly and raises `TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for |` on Python 3.9 (still a supported interpreter per README). `from __future__ import annotations` does not help here. This would fail collection of the whole async command test module. Use `typing.Union[redis.Redis, redis.RedisCluster]` (or quote it and guard under TYPE_CHECKING).

`xnack` calls `self.execute_command("XNACK", *pieces)` without `keys=[name]`, unlike every neighbouring stream command (e.g. `xlen` uses `keys=[name]`). Without the `keys` hint the cluster client cannot statically determine the target slot for this brand-new command and must fall back to a `COMMAND GETKEYS` round-trip (or fail for servers whose command table the client hasn't refreshed). Pass `keys=[name]` for consistency and correct/efficient cluster routing.

Argument tokens are inconsistently encoded: `"IDS"` is a str while `b"RETRYCOUNT"` and `b"FORCE"` are bytes within the same `pieces` list. Pick one representation (the surrounding code uses bytes literals for modifier keywords).

`mode` validation is strictly case-sensitive (`mode not in {"SILENT", "FAIL", "FATAL"}`), so a lowercase value that Redis itself would accept raises DataError. Other commands in this module normalise such modifiers (e.g. via `.upper()`); consider doing the same to avoid a surprising client-side rejection.

`_ClusterNodePoolAdapter.get_connection()` acquires a node connection and immediately awaits `connection.connect()` without first calling `connection.disconnect_if_needed()`. ClusterNode's lazy-reconnect protocol requires every borrower (see `ClusterNode.execute_command`/`execute_pipeline`) to run `disconnect_if_needed()` before sending and before returning the connection to `_free`; connections invalidated by a topology change or maintenance push are only flagged via `mark_for_reconnect()` and are dropped at that point. By skipping it, a PubSub can subscribe on a connection that was already marked stale and will keep it for the whole life of the subscription. Mirror the node's protocol: call `connection.disconnect_if_needed()` in `get_connection()` (and in `release()`) before handing the connection out / putting it back.

Removing the module-level `pytestmark = pytest.mark.onlycluster` silently un-marks every test in this ~4600-line module that the diff does not explicitly re-mark. Only six classes get `@pytest.mark.onlycluster` here, while other cluster-dependent classes remain unmarked (e.g. the class that ends just above `TestRedisClusterObj` around line 303, and the real-cluster pubsub tests around line 4609 that use a live `RedisCluster` fixture). Those will now be collected and fail in the standalone (non-cluster) CI run. Either keep the module-level marker and add `@pytest.mark.fixed_client` only to the mock-based classes, or verify that *every* remaining class/function got a marker.

Shard PubSub objects created here now borrow a connection from the ClusterNode's own pool. `node_pubsub_mapping` entries are dropped as soon as the per-node PubSub reports `subscribed is False` (on sunsubscribe) without `aclose()` being awaited, so the borrowed connection is never handed back via `ClusterNode.release()` and, because `ClusterNode._connections` never removes entries, it permanently consumes one of the node's `max_connections` slots. With the previous detached pool this only leaked a throwaway pool object. Consider closing the shard PubSub (or releasing its connection) when the mapping entry is evicted.

`test_disconnect_tolerates_shard_pubsub_with_no_connection` asserts that `ClusterPubSub.disconnect()` skips shard PubSub entries whose `connection` is None, but the diff does not add such a guard to `redis/cluster.py`. If the current implementation still does `pubsub.connection.disconnect()` unconditionally, this test fails with `AttributeError` on the `pending_pubsub` entry; if the guard already exists, the test is unrelated to this PR. Please confirm the source path actually supports the asserted behaviour.

`_ClusterNodePoolAdapter.get_connection()` acquires a connection from the node but skips the node's lazy-reconnect contract. `ClusterNode.execute_command()`/`execute_pipeline()` always call `await self.disconnect_if_needed(connection)` right after `acquire_connection()`, because connections flagged via `mark_for_reconnect()` (topology change, failover, `set_nodes()`, ConnectionError handling) are only recycled at acquire time. Since the adapter goes straight to `connection.connect()` — a no-op when the socket is still `is_connected` — a PubSub can subscribe over a socket the cluster has explicitly marked stale (e.g. a demoted primary or a connection carrying stale READONLY state) and keep it for the whole subscription lifetime. Add `await self._node.disconnect_if_needed(connection)` before `connect()`.

In the failure path of `_ClusterNodePoolAdapter.get_connection()`, `await connection.disconnect()` is executed before `self._node.release(connection)`. `AbstractConnection.disconnect()` can itself raise (e.g. `TimeoutError` when closing exceeds `socket_connect_timeout`), in which case `release()` is never reached: the connection stays in `node._connections` but never returns to `_free`, permanently consuming a slot against `ClusterNode.max_connections`. Wrap the disconnect in `try/finally` (or release first) so the connection is always returned to the node.

`test_disconnect_tolerates_shard_pubsub_with_no_connection` asserts that `ClusterPubSub.disconnect()` skips shard pubsubs whose `connection` is still `None`, but this diff does not touch `ClusterPubSub.disconnect()` in redis/cluster.py. If that method still does `pubsub.connection.disconnect()` unguarded, the test raises `AttributeError` on the first (pending) entry and never reaches the `active_pubsub` assertion. Please confirm the None-guard exists in production code, or add it as part of this change.

`ClusterPubSub.get_redis_connection()`'s docstring/comment still claims the pubsub connection comes from "its own connection pool" and that this "avoids the connection pool resource leak that would occur if we called node.acquire_connection() without releasing". After this refactor the connection is acquired precisely via `ClusterNode.acquire_connection()` through `_ClusterNodePoolAdapter`, so the rationale is now misleading and should be updated.

PEP 604 union syntax in a runtime-evaluated annotation: `Mapping[ChannelT, Callable | None]` is in a function signature and this module has no `from __future__ import annotations`. On Python 3.9 (still supported per README: "redis-py 6.2.0 supports Python 3.9+"), `typing.Callable | None` raises `TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for |` at import time. Since `redis/client.py` and `redis/asyncio/client.py` now import this module unconditionally, `import redis` would fail entirely on 3.9. Use `Optional[Callable]` (or add the `__future__` import).

`test_standalone_pubsub_on_connect_batches_shard_channels` is missing `@pytest.mark.onlynoncluster` (the sync counterpart in tests/test_pubsub.py has it). In the cluster test run the `pubsub` fixture yields a `ClusterPubSub`, whose newly added `_resubscribe_shard_channels` groups by slot, so the two different-slot channels produce two `ssubscribe` calls and `assert len(calls) == 1` fails.

The integration test hardcodes channel names ("resub-a-0"/"resub-b-0") and then *asserts* that they land on different slots of the same master. On any cluster topology other than the assumed 3-master default (e.g. a different shard count or slot assignment) this fails with a confusing assertion error instead of skipping. Either derive channel names dynamically (scan for two names whose slots are owned by the same node) or `pytest.skip()` when the precondition does not hold. Same issue in the async copy in tests/test_asyncio/test_pubsub.py.

`Mapping[ChannelT, Callable | None]` uses PEP 604 union syntax in a function signature that is evaluated at import time, and the module has no `from __future__ import annotations`. On Python 3.9 (still a supported version per README: "redis-py 6.2.0 supports Python 3.9+") `typing.Callable | None` raises `TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for |`, so importing `redis.commands.helpers` — and therefore `redis.client` / the whole package — fails. Use `Optional[Callable]`/`typing.Union` or add the `__future__` import. (`tuple[...]`/`list[...]`/`dict[...]` are fine on 3.9, only the `|` union is the problem.)

Binding the slot-aware resubscribe via `MethodType(ClusterPubSub._resubscribe_shard_channels, pubsub)` hard-codes the base class implementation, so a subclass of `ClusterPubSub` that overrides `_resubscribe_shard_channels` will be silently ignored on the per-node PubSub instances (same in `redis/asyncio/cluster.py`). Using `type(self)._resubscribe_shard_channels` (or a dedicated per-node PubSub subclass) would preserve normal override semantics; the per-instance attribute also creates a reference cycle between the PubSub and its bound method.

The cluster integration test asserts environment topology (`assert r.keyslot(ch_a) != r.keyslot(ch_b)` and `assert r.get_node_from_key(ch_a).name == r.get_node_from_key(ch_b).name`) with hard-coded channel names tuned to the default 3-master test cluster. On any other slot distribution this fails as an error rather than skipping, producing false negatives. Prefer deriving two channels that map to the same node at runtime (or `pytest.skip` when none can be found). Same pattern in tests/test_asyncio/test_pubsub.py::TestClusterPubSubResubscribe.

`unregister_listeners` is added to `EventDispatcherInterface` as an `@abstractmethod`. `EventDispatcher`/`EventDispatcherInterface` are part of the public surface (users can pass a custom `event_dispatcher=` into clients and the multi-db config), so any third-party class deriving from this ABC stops being instantiable (`TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class ... with abstract method unregister_listeners`) after upgrading. Either make the new method non-abstract with a default no-op/raise implementation, or document it as a breaking interface change in the release notes.

`NodesManager.move_slot()` is converted from a regular method into a coroutine purely so it can `await dispatch_async`. This silently breaks any caller that is not updated: an un-awaited `move_slot(e)` returns a coroutine, performs no slot update at all, and only surfaces as a "coroutine was never awaited" RuntimeWarning. Two internal call sites are updated here, but the change also breaks external/subclass callers of this public (non-underscore) method and diverges from the sync twin's signature. Consider keeping `move_slot` synchronous and scheduling the dispatch (e.g. `asyncio.get_running_loop().create_task(...)` / a small async wrapper), or at minimum audit every remaining `move_slot(` call site in the async stack (pipeline/transaction strategies, maint-notification paths) for a missing `await`.

The reconciliation worker mutates and tears down per-node PubSub objects while the consumer thread reads them without any shared lock: `get_sharded_message()` deliberately calls `_sharded_message_generator()` / `pubsub.get_message()` outside `_shard_state_lock`, while `reinitialize_shard_subscriptions()`'s GC block calls `pubsub.reset()` (which disconnects the connection and releases it back to the pool) and pops entries from `node_pubsub_mapping` under the lock. A consumer blocked in `get_message()` on that same per-node pubsub can therefore have its connection disconnected and returned to the pool underneath it (raising `RuntimeError: pubsub connection not set` at best, and handing an in-use pub/sub connection to another pool user at worst), and the round-robin `_pubsubs_generator` can observe `node_pubsub_mapping` changing size mid-iteration. The same interleaving exists in the async twin at await points. Either take `_shard_state_lock` around the per-node read, or hand off teardown of a pubsub to the reader (as the sunsubscribe branch already does) instead of doing it from the worker.

The new `dispatch(AfterSlotsCacheRefreshEvent())` in `NodesManager.initialize()` is indented inside the `with self._lock:` block, so arbitrary listener code now runs while the topology lock is held. This contradicts the discipline the same PR establishes in `move_slot()` ("Dispatch outside the lock so listeners can acquire their own locks without risk of deadlock") and the async counterpart, where the dispatch is placed after the locked block. The bundled listener acquires `ClusterPubSub._shard_state_lock` here, so any code path that holds `_shard_state_lock` and then needs the NodesManager lock creates a lock-order inversion. Move the dispatch out of the `with self._lock:` block for consistency and safety.

The class-level `@pytest.mark.onlycluster` is removed from `TestNodesManager` in favour of per-method markers (same change in tests/test_asyncio/test_cluster.py). Every remaining method in this large class must now carry `onlycluster`/`fixed_client`; any method left unmarked will be collected in the standalone (non-cluster) CI job and fail, and the failure only shows up in that job. Please confirm the audit covers all methods of the class (including any not touched by this diff), or keep the class-level marker and add the narrower marker only to the new mock-based tests.

`_unregister_slots_cache_listener` is a purely synchronous helper duplicated byte-for-byte from redis/cluster.py. Per the module split convention (redis/asyncio/cluster.py should only hold await-specific code and import protocol-agnostic helpers from redis.cluster), import the sync helper instead of copying it so the two copies cannot drift.

`NodesManager.initialize()` dispatches `AfterSlotsCacheRefreshEvent` while still holding `_initialization_lock` (the dispatch is inside the `with self._initialization_lock:` body), and the sync `ClusterPubSub.on_slots_changed()` listener acquires `_shard_state_lock` synchronously in the dispatching thread just to lazily build the executor. `reinitialize_shard_subscriptions()` holds that *same* lock for the entire pass, including per-channel connect/SSUBSCRIBE network I/O (redis-py defaults `socket_connect_timeout`/`socket_timeout` to None). So while a reconcile pass is in flight against a slow or hung node, every subsequent `NodesManager.initialize()` blocks in the dispatch call while holding `_initialization_lock`, stalling topology refresh for the whole client — exactly what off-loading to a worker thread was meant to avoid (the async path avoids it because `on_slots_changed` only calls `asyncio.create_task`). Guard the lazy executor creation / `_reconcile_futures` bookkeeping with a small dedicated lock instead of `_shard_state_lock`.

Per-node pubsubs are now closed and removed from `node_pubsub_mapping` in three new places — the `sunsubscribe` branch of `get_sharded_message()`, `_migrate_shard_channel()` (old node no longer in topology) and the GC loop at the end of `reinitialize_shard_subscriptions()` — but none of them recreates `_pubsubs_generator`. As the diff itself documents for `aclose()`/`reset()`, `yield from current_nodes` captures a snapshot of `node_pubsub_mapping.values()`, so a generator suspended mid-`yield from` will still yield an already-closed pubsub that it had not yet consumed from that snapshot (e.g. one dropped by the background reconcile task, or dropped while the caller polls with `target_node=`). In asyncio, `PubSub.get_message()` on a closed pubsub reaches `parse_response()` with `self.connection is None` and raises `RuntimeError("pubsub connection not set: ...")` out of `get_sharded_message()`; the sync counterpart silently burns the round-robin iteration and starves other nodes for that call. These drop sites need the same generator recreation applied in `aclose()`/`reset()` (or the generator should re-snapshot on every yield).

`unregister_listeners` is added as an `@abstractmethod` on the public `EventDispatcherInterface`. Any third-party (or in-repo) implementation of that interface that does not define the new method becomes uninstantiable (`TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class ...`), which is a breaking change for downstream code that passes a custom `event_dispatcher=` into `Redis`/`RedisCluster`. Consider adding it as a concrete no-op/default on the interface (non-abstract) so existing implementations keep working.

`_migrate_shard_channel()` (both the sync and async copies) builds a kwarg key via `self.encoder.decode(channel, force=True)` whenever a handler is registered. For shard channel names that are not valid UTF-8 this raises `UnicodeDecodeError` — the same bug class recently fixed for reconnect resubscription (issue #3912, covered by `test_resubscribe_binary_channel_on_reconnection`). It is not caught by the `(ConnectionError, TimeoutError, OSError)` handler in `reinitialize_shard_subscriptions()`, so a single binary-named channel aborts the whole reconcile pass (including the trailing per-node GC) on every slots-cache change. Prefer subscribing positionally and assigning the handler into the new pubsub's `shard_channels` instead of decoding the key.

`AsyncSearchCommands.profile()` was deleted (the whole `async def profile` block between `aggregate` and `spellcheck`) and no replacement was added. Since `AsyncSearchCommands` subclasses `SearchCommands`, `await r.ft().profile(q)` now dispatches to the synchronous implementation, which does `res = self.execute_command(*cmd)` (a coroutine, never awaited) and immediately hands it to `self._parse_results(PROFILE_CMD, res, ...)`. The parser then calls `res.get("Results")` / indexes it, raising AttributeError/TypeError plus a "coroutine was never awaited" warning. FT.PROFILE is broken for all asyncio clients.

`aggregate()` and `profile()` lost their `if isinstance(raw, Pipeline): return raw` guards, but still call `self._parse_results(...)` with `query=` in kwargs (so the early-return in `_parse_results` does not trigger). When these methods are invoked on the search `Pipeline` (`client.ft().pipeline()`), `execute_command` returns the pipeline itself, so the callback receives the Pipeline object: `_get_aggregate_result` does `raw[1:]` and `_parse_aggregate_resp3` does `data.get("total_results", 0)`, both of which blow up on a Pipeline. Note `search()` was kept pipeline-aware in the same file, so this looks like an oversight; pipelined FT.AGGREGATE/FT.CURSOR/FT.PROFILE now raise instead of queueing.

Changing the constructor default from `protocol=3` to `protocol=None` (and forwarding it verbatim into `connection_kwargs`) means `ConnectionPool.get_protocol()` now returns `None` for a default client while the connection actually negotiates RESP3. Callers that branch on `get_protocol() in [3, "3"]` — notably `PubSub.__init__`'s `health_check_response` selection in both `redis/client.py` and `redis/asyncio/client.py` — silently take the RESP2 path over a RESP3 connection, so health-check replies are no longer recognised and are surfaced to the user as ordinary messages. Either normalise `None` once (e.g. `get_protocol()` returning `DEFAULT_RESP_VERSION`) or switch the remaining `in [3, "3"]` sites to `check_protocol_version()` as was done for the cache/maint-notifications checks.

`_TimeSeriesBase.pipeline()` now passes `response_callbacks=self._MODULE_CALLBACKS` instead of the client's callback table. Two problems: (1) core-command callbacks are gone, so a TimeSeries pipeline returns raw replies for non-TS commands (e.g. `pipe.set()` -> b"OK" instead of True, `pipe.hgetall()` -> flat list); (2) the module's own dict is handed over uncopied, so `Pipeline.set_response_callback()` mutates state shared with the module instance and every other pipeline. JSON (`dict(self.client.response_callbacks)`) and Search (`dict(response_callbacks)`) do this correctly in the same PR.

`_RedisCallbacksRESP3Unified` is built from `_RedisCallbacksRESP3`, which (after this diff) no longer carries the BGREWRITEAOF/BGSAVE `lambda r: True`, `DEBUG OBJECT: parse_debug_object`, or value-typed XINFO/CONFIG-GET handling, whereas `_RedisCallbacksRESP2Unified` inherits all of them from `_RedisCallbacksRESP2`. With `legacy_responses=False` the same command therefore still returns protocol-dependent shapes: `bgsave()` -> True (RESP2) vs status string (RESP3); `debug_object()` -> dict vs raw string; `xinfo_groups()` -> bytes values vs native ints; `config_get()` -> bytes keys/values vs str keys/values. That contradicts the stated contract of unified responses (and the new docs/spec tables), and none of these are covered by the matrix tests.

`TSInfo.__init__` takes the dict branch for every RESP3-wire reply (unified and default-legacy modes both route TS.INFO through `TSInfo`), but looks keys up with `str` literals (`response.get("sourceKey")`, `"rules"`, `"labels"`, ...). With the default `decode_responses=False`, a RESP3 map arrives with bytes keys, so every attribute silently becomes `None` and `labels`/`rules` become `{}`. Normalise the keys first (e.g. `{nativestr(k): v for k, v in args.items()}`, as `redis/commands/bf/info.py::_parse_info_args` does) before populating the attributes.

`parse_memory_stats_unified` drops `decode_string_values=True`, so RESP2 bulk-string fields such as `allocator-frag-ratio` / `rss-overhead-ratio` / `peak.percentage` come back as `bytes` when `decode_responses=False`, while the RESP3 unified path (`parse_memory_stats_resp3`) yields native floats for the same fields. Unifying MEMORY STATS requires converting these to the RESP3 native type, not just skipping the decode step; as written the unified shape is still protocol-dependent (and the new docs claim "numeric values use native types"). The same float-vs-str divergence exists between `parse_memory_stats` (RESP2 legacy) and `parse_memory_stats_resp3` used for default-legacy.

The sync `AbstractConnection.__init__` now only upgrades `_RESP2Parser -> _RESP3Parser`; the `protocol == 2 and parser_class == _RESP3Parser -> _RESP2Parser` downgrade was removed, while `redis/asyncio/connection.py` keeps both directions (and even gains a test for the downgrade). An explicit `Connection(protocol=2, parser_class=_RESP3Parser)` will now send `HELLO 2` while parsing with the RESP3 parser. Please keep the sync and async reconciliation symmetric.

`AsyncSearchCommands.profile()` was deleted. `AsyncSearchCommands` subclasses `SearchCommands`, so async clients now resolve `ft().profile(...)` to the *synchronous* implementation, which does `res = self.execute_command(*cmd)` (a coroutine on async clients) and immediately passes it to `self._parse_results(PROFILE_CMD, res, ...)`. The parser will index/`.get()` a coroutine object (TypeError/AttributeError), and the method is no longer awaitable. This silently breaks a public async API (`FT.PROFILE`). Either keep the async override or make the shared implementation protocol-agnostic.

`aggregate()` (and `profile()` a few lines below) lost the `if isinstance(raw, Pipeline): return raw` early return, but still call `self._parse_results(...)` unconditionally. Inside a Search pipeline `execute_command()` returns the pipeline itself, so the parser is now handed a `Pipeline` object: e.g. `_parse_aggregate_resp3` calls `data.get("total_results", 0)`, which on a pipeline queues a spurious Redis `GET` command and then fails when iterating `data.get("results", [])`. `search()`/`hybrid_search()` still keep the guard, so this is an inconsistent regression for `p.aggregate(...)` / `p.profile(...)`. Restore the pipeline short-circuit (the registered pipeline response callbacks handle parsing at `execute()`).

`_TimeSeriesBase.pipeline()` now passes `response_callbacks=self._MODULE_CALLBACKS`, i.e. only the TimeSeries module callbacks and by reference. Two consequences: (a) core Redis commands issued on a `ts().pipeline()` get no response post-processing (e.g. `HGETALL`, `INFO`, `SET` return raw wire values), and (b) the pipeline shares the module callback dict, so `set_response_callback()` on the pipeline mutates the module-level mapping. The JSON module in this same diff uses `dict(self.client.response_callbacks)`; the TimeSeries pipeline should be consistent (copy of the client's callbacks).

The sync `Connection` protocol/parser reconciliation now only upgrades `_RESP2Parser` → `_RESP3Parser` when `protocol == 3`; the reverse branch (`protocol == 2` with an explicitly supplied `_RESP3Parser`) was removed, while `redis/asyncio/connection.py` in this same diff keeps both directions. Constructing a sync connection with `protocol=2, parser_class=_RESP3Parser` now leaves a RESP3 parser on a RESP2 handshake, producing protocol-mismatch parse errors. Keep the two branches symmetric with the async implementation.

`parse_cluster_shards_unified` is not protocol-independent for the `slots` field: the RESP2 branch pairs the flat slot array into `[(start, end), ...]`, while the RESP3 branch returns the server's flat array (`[start, end, ...]`) unchanged. Since the whole point of `legacy_responses=False` is that the same command yields the same Python shape on both wires (and `docs/unified_responses.rst` documents CLUSTER SHARDS only as "string structural keys"), the slot representation should be normalized in both branches.

`def list_or_args(keys: Any, args: Iterable[Any] | None) -> List[Any]:` uses a PEP 604 union in an annotation that is evaluated at import time. This module is imported unconditionally (redis/commands/core.py does `from .helpers import list_or_args`), and the library still supports Python 3.9 (see README), where `Iterable[Any] | None` raises `TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for |` and breaks `import redis` entirely. The previous signature used typing-style aliases, so unless this module already has `from __future__ import annotations` at the top, use `Optional[Iterable[Any]]` instead.

`bytearray` is now accepted at runtime here (and converted for hiredis in connection.py, plus exercised by the new tests), but the type aliases in redis/typing.py were not updated: `EncodedT = Union[bytes, memoryview]`, so `EncodableT`/`FieldT`/`KeyT` still exclude `bytearray`. Since the point of this PR is to make the hash command hints match the supported argument types, calls like `r.hset(name, bytearray(b"f"), bytearray(b"v"))` remain type errors for mypy users even though they are now supported and tested. Add `bytearray` to `EncodedT`/`_StringLikeT`.

The new `hmget` assertions with a `memoryview`/`bytearray` field depend on `list_or_args` treating those as a single field. The helper only special-cases `isinstance(keys, (bytes, str))` and otherwise does `list(keys)`, which expands a memoryview/bytearray into a list of per-byte ints (so `HMGET key 102 105 ...` would be sent). Either these assertions fail, or `list_or_args` needs the same widening as the encoder — please verify and, if needed, extend the isinstance check in redis/commands/helpers.py (same applies to the asyncio test).

`Encoder.encode` now accepts `bytearray` at runtime (and the new tests assert `hset`/`hget`/`hmget` work with it), but the type aliases used by the newly-tightened hash hints were not updated: `redis/typing.py` still defines `EncodedT = Union[bytes, memoryview]`, so `EncodableT`/`FieldT`/`KeyT` exclude `bytearray`. Callers passing a `bytearray` field/value will still be flagged by type checkers even though it is now supported, which contradicts the stated goal of "hints with all supported arg types". Either add `bytearray` to `EncodedT`/`_StringLikeT` in `redis/typing.py` or leave the encoder unchanged.

This rebuilds the argument tuple with a generator + per-arg `isinstance` check on every single command packed via hiredis (the hot path), and `bytes(arg)` copies the whole buffer for `memoryview` arguments — defeating the reason callers pass a `memoryview` in the first place (redis-py deliberately avoids copying large memoryview values in `PythonRespSerializer`). Consider converting only when needed (e.g. lazily on the `TypeError` fallback, or guarded by `any(isinstance(a, (bytearray, memoryview)) for a in args)`) so the common all-bytes/str case pays nothing.

`encode()` now returns `bytearray` unchanged, but `decode()` only normalizes `memoryview`/`bytes`, so `encoder.decode(value, force=True)` on encoder output returns the raw `bytearray` instead of a `str` (e.g. the ACL error messages in `commands/core.py` would render `bytearray(b'...')`). Related: `bytearray` is unhashable, so encoded values used as dict keys (PubSub channel maps via `dict.fromkeys(map(encoder.encode, args))`, CSC `CacheKey`) now raise an opaque `TypeError: unhashable type: 'bytearray'` where a clear `DataError` was raised before. Consider converting `bytearray` to `bytes` in `encode()` instead of passing it through.

`increx` targets a pre-GA server (tests gate on `skip_if_server_version_lt("8.7.0")` while CI's current version is 8.6.1 / 8.8-rc1) but is not decorated with `@experimental_method()` from `redis.utils`, unlike the other unreleased commands in this module (`delex`, `digest`, `digest_local`). Without the decorator no instability warning is emitted, and the method looks like a stable, supported API.

`_wait_for_bgsave` polls `INFO persistence` only on `r.get_default_node()`, but `BGSAVE` in the cluster client fans out to all primaries. Combined with removing the `ResponseError` ("Background save already in progress") tolerance, the test can still fail when a non-default primary is mid-save. Poll all primaries (e.g. `target_nodes=RedisCluster.PRIMARIES`) or keep the tolerant except-branch.

The `increx` docstring does not document the `ex`/`px`/`exat`/`pxat`/`persist` parameters and omits the customary trailing "Available since Redis X.Y" / "For more information, see https://redis.io/commands/increx" lines that every neighbouring command (e.g. `incrbyfloat`, `msetex`, `getex`) carries.

The `increx` docstring omits conventions used by every neighbouring command in this file: there is no `For more information, see https://redis.io/commands/increx` link, no "Available since Redis <x.y>" note (the tests gate on 8.7.0, so the version requirement is not discoverable from the API docs), and no description of the returned two-element list ([new value, actual increment]). Since the public docs are generated from these docstrings, this should be filled in.

`_wait_for_bgsave` only polls `INFO persistence` on the default node, but `RedisCluster.bgsave()` is routed to all primaries. The previously present `except ResponseError: "Background save already in progress"` tolerance was removed, so a save still running on any non-default primary will now surface as a hard failure instead of being tolerated. Either wait across `r.get_primaries()` (matching the command's fan-out) or keep the ResponseError tolerance.

The reworked `test_concurrent_initialize_and_move_slot` uses the same 5s timeout for `t2.join(timeout=5)` and for `allow_initialize_to_finish.wait(timeout=5)` inside the paused `check_slots_coverage`. If `move_slot` blocks on the same lock/epoch that the paused `initialize()` holds, the join will time out at roughly the same instant the pause is released, and the initialize thread can raise the "Timed out waiting for move_slot worker" error, appending to `errors` and failing `assert len(errors) == 0`. Use clearly different timeouts (release the pause before joining t2) so the release always wins. Note also that replacing the 100-iteration randomized loop with a single deterministic interleaving where move_slot is likely serialized behind the initialize lock significantly weakens the race coverage this test was written for.

`TimeoutError` in this module resolves to `redis.exceptions.TimeoutError` (imported at the top of the file), not the builtin, so this watchdog raises a Redis protocol exception from test scaffolding. Use `AssertionError`/`RuntimeError` (or `builtins.TimeoutError`) to avoid confusing the failure with a real client timeout and to avoid any chance of it being swallowed by the retry-on-TimeoutError paths in `NodesManager.initialize`.

All 18 `ArrayCommands` methods target a pre-GA server (PR text says Redis 8.8.0 preview; tests gate on `skip_if_server_version_lt("8.7.2")`), but none carries `@experimental_method()` from `redis.utils`. Per repo convention (see `delex`, `digest`, `digest_local`), commands for a not-yet-GA server feature must be decorated so an instability warning is emitted; otherwise these appear to users as stable, supported APIs.

None of the new read-only commands passes the `keys=` option to `execute_command` (`arget`, `armget`, `argetrange`, `arscan`, `argrep`, `arcount`, `arlen`, `arinfo`, `arnext`, `arlastitems`, `arop`). Every other read command in this module supplies `keys=[name]` (or `keys=args`) so the cluster client can route the request and the client-side cache can track key dependencies; omitting it silently breaks client-side caching invalidation for these commands.

`parse_arinfo` only reshapes list-vs-map; it does not normalize value types, so the promised consistent `dict[str, int]` does not hold for `ARINFO ... FULL`. Fields such as `avg-dense-size`, `avg-dense-fill`, `avg-sparse-size` are doubles: RESP3 yields `float`, while RESP2 delivers them as bulk strings, which `pairs_to_dict(response, decode_keys=True)` (no `decode_string_values=True`) leaves as `bytes` when `decode_responses=False`. Either convert these fields to native numbers in the RESP2 branch or drop the `dict[str, int]` annotation on `arinfo`; the new tests only assert field presence, so this divergence is untested.

Command tokens are emitted as bytes literals (`b"LIMIT"` in `arscan`/`argrep`, `b"WITHVALUES"`, `b"NOCASE"`, `b"FULL"` in `arinfo`, `b"REV"` in `arlastitems`), while surrounding commands in this module use plain `str` tokens. Keep the token style consistent with the rest of core.py.

No client-side argument validation: `armset` with an empty `mapping` sends `ARMSET key` with no pairs, and `arset`/`armget`/`ardel`/`ardelrange`/`argrep` with no values/indices/ranges/predicates likewise build malformed commands that only fail server-side. Convention in this module is to raise `redis.exceptions.DataError` for empty collections before dispatch (cf. `hset`, `mset`); `arop` with `ArrayAggregateOperations.MATCH` and `value=None` has the same problem (the test asserts a server `ResponseError` instead).

The new command docstrings end with only the `For more information, see https://redis.io/commands/...` line; house style in this module also includes the `Available since Redis X.Y` line (see `incrbyfloat`, `msetex`, `getex`), which is especially useful here since these commands require a preview server.

Sync/async test parity is uneven: the sync suite adds seven `argetrange` cases (reversed range, single index, empty indices, missing key, out of bounds, ...) while the async suite only has `test_argetrange_returns_values_in_range`. Mirror the sync cases so the async path gets equivalent coverage.

`parse_arinfo` only normalises the *keys* of the ARINFO reply; values are passed through untouched. The `ARINFO ... FULL` reply includes non-integer statistics (`avg-dense-size`, `avg-dense-fill`, `avg-sparse-size`). On a RESP2 wire a double is delivered as a bulk string (`b"0.75"` / `"0.75"` when decoding), while on a RESP3 wire it arrives as a native `float`. So the value types still diverge per protocol, contrary to the PR's claim of a single `dict[str, int]` shape for all five (protocol × legacy_responses) modes, and contrary to the annotation on `ArrayCommands.arinfo` (`dict[str, int]`). Either coerce the numeric fields explicitly in the parser (as `parse_client_info`/`parse_acl_log` do) or register protocol-specific overlays in `_RedisCallbacksRESP2Unified`/`_RedisCallbacksRESP3*`. The new tests only assert `field in info` for the FULL fields, so they cannot catch this.

None of the new methods validate that the caller supplied any data before building the command: `armset(name, {})` sends bare `ARMSET key`, `arset`/`arinsert`/`arring`/`armget`/`ardel` with no varargs send a key-only command, `ardelrange(name)` with no ranges likewise, `argrep(..., predicates=[])` sends no predicate, and `arop(..., ArrayAggregateOperations.MATCH)` without `value` silently omits the required argument. All of these surface as an opaque server-side `ResponseError` instead of the client-side `DataError` this codebase raises for the equivalent situations (`zadd({})`, `hset` without data, `mset({})`). Consider adding the same up-front `DataError` checks.

The `arget` implementation signature is hand-wrapped (`def arget(self, name: KeyT, index: int) -> (bytes | str | None) | Awaitable[\n    bytes | str | None\n]:`), which is not the formatter's canonical output — the formatter splits the parameter list first and keeps the return annotation on the closing line. `invoke linters` (format check) will fail on this; run `invoke linters-fix`.

`redis/typing.py` has no `from __future__ import annotations` (the diff even deletes the commented-out line), so the new dataclass field annotation `handler: PubSubHandler | None = None` is evaluated at class-creation time. `PubSubHandler` is a `typing.Callable[...]` alias, and `_GenericAlias.__or__` (PEP 604) only exists on Python 3.10+; on 3.9 this raises `TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for |`. Because `redis/typing.py` is imported unconditionally by `redis/client.py`, this breaks `import redis` entirely on the still-documented minimum Python (README: 6.2.0 supports 3.9+). The same hazard is introduced in the new signatures `*args: ChannelT | Subscription` in redis/client.py, redis/asyncio/client.py, redis/cluster.py, redis/asyncio/cluster.py, redis/multidb/client.py and redis/asyncio/multidb/client.py, and in the return annotations of `parse_pubsub_subscriptions`/`pubsub_subscription_args` in redis/commands/helpers.py. Use `Optional[...]`/`Union[...]` or add the future import.

`parse_pubsub_subscriptions` unconditionally does `list_or_args(args[0], args[1:])`, but the async `subscribe`/`psubscribe` it replaces used `list_or_args((args[0],), args[1:])` (first arg wrapped). `list_or_args` only treats `bytes`/`str` as a single key, so a `bytearray` or `memoryview` channel name passed as the first positional argument is now expanded via `list(keys)` into per-byte ints — `await p.subscribe(bytearray(b"chan"))` silently subscribes to "99", "104", ... instead of the channel. The same mangling now happens on the async reconnect replay path, since `Encoder.encode` keeps `memoryview` keys intact in `self.channels`/`self.patterns`. This is a behaviour regression for the async client (the sync twin already had it) and it contradicts the new `*args: ChannelT | Subscription` hint, which includes `memoryview`. Widen the single-name check to `(bytes, bytearray, memoryview, str, Subscription)` before falling back to `list_or_args`.

The comment above `_migrate_shard_channel` still explains the removed decoding logic ("...a text key only when we must pass it as a kwarg (handler present)"), which no longer matches the code now that a positional `Subscription(channel, handler)` is passed. Same stale comment in `redis/asyncio/cluster.py::_migrate_shard_channel`.

Marker parity with the sync twin is broken: `test_resubscribe_binary_channel_with_handler_on_reconnection` and `test_binary_channel_message_handler_with_subscription` carry `@pytest.mark.onlynoncluster` in tests/test_pubsub.py but not here, so in the cluster job the shared `pubsub`/`r` fixtures yield `ClusterPubSub`/`RedisCluster` and these tests exercise a different code path (node-bound pub/sub, cluster-wide publish, cluster reconnect) than the sync versions the author deliberately excluded. Add the same markers so the async copies stay a mirror of the sync ones.

Stale comment: the lines above `_migrate_shard_channel`'s subscribe call still explain that the channel is decoded "to a text key only when we must pass it as a kwarg (handler present)", but the code now passes `Subscription(channel, handler)` positionally and never decodes. The same stale comment remains in `redis/asyncio/cluster.py` (`_migrate_shard_channel`, ~line 3782). Please update both so the rationale matches the new code.

`parse_pubsub_subscriptions` and `pubsub_subscription_args` are new shared helpers with no docstrings, while the `partition_pubsub_subscriptions_by_handler` they replace documented exactly why binary names must not be turned into keyword keys. That rationale (and the contract of the new `Subscription` return form) is now undocumented, which the contributing guide asks for (docstrings, Google style). Also worth noting: `parse_pubsub_subscriptions` uses `list_or_args(args[0], ...)`, which changes async `subscribe`/`psubscribe` behaviour (a non-str iterable first argument is now expanded instead of treated as one channel) — intentional harmonization, but it should be stated somewhere.

`Subscription` is only accepted by `subscribe`/`psubscribe`/`ssubscribe`; the matching `unsubscribe`/`punsubscribe`/`sunsubscribe` still run their positional args through `_normalize_keys`/`encode`, so the natural symmetric call `p.unsubscribe(Subscription(b"\x80\x81", handler))` fails with `DataError: Invalid input of type: 'Subscription'`. Either accept `Subscription` there (using `.name`) or document explicitly that unsubscribes must be done by raw name.

The new `-> None` annotations contradict the bodies: `PubSub.subscribe`/`psubscribe`/`ssubscribe` still end with `return ret_val`, and the multidb wrappers (`redis/multidb/client.py`, `redis/asyncio/multidb/client.py`) `return self._client.command_executor.execute_pubsub_method(...)`. Values happen to be `None` at runtime, but a type checker flags `return <value>` in a `-> None` function; drop the returns or annotate the real type.

`_socket_can_read()` replaces the previous `recv`-based readiness probe with `select.select()`. On Linux/macOS, `select.select()` raises `ValueError: filedescriptor out of range in select()` for any file descriptor >= FD_SETSIZE (1024), and `ValueError` for a negative fd (already-closed socket). This makes the sync hiredis readiness check (pool checkout `can_read()`, PubSub `get_message(timeout=...)`) blow up in processes that hold many open descriptors — and `ValueError` is not one of the transport errors the connection layer normalizes to `ConnectionError`/`TimeoutError`, so it escapes to callers as an unexpected exception type. Prefer `selectors.PollSelector`/`select.poll()` (or keep the non-destructive check based on `recv` with `MSG_PEEK`/reader state) so there is no fd-count ceiling.

`AsyncBaseParser.can_read_destructive` is decorated with both `@deprecated_function(...)` and `@abstractmethod`, so it stays a *required* override for every subclass while simultaneously being announced as deprecated. That contradicts the stated migration path ("custom async parsers must implement can_read()"): implementers now have to provide both methods, and the abstract body is `pass`, so a subclass delegating via `await super().can_read_destructive()` silently returns `None` instead of failing. Both in-tree parsers already define the shim `return await self.can_read()`; hoist that concrete implementation into `AsyncBaseParser` and mark only `can_read()` abstract. (The stacking also depends on `functools.wraps` copying `__isabstractmethod__` through `__dict__`, which is fragile/unobvious.)

`BaseParser.on_disconnect`/`on_connect` change from concrete methods raising `NotImplementedError` to `@abstractmethod` with `pass` bodies. Since `BaseParser` subclasses `ABC`, any third-party parser passed via `parser_class=` that previously omitted one of these (legal as long as it was never called) now fails at *instantiation* with `TypeError`. This runtime-breaking change is not covered by the PR's migration note (which mentions only `can_read`). Additionally, the `pass` bodies mean `super().on_connect(...)` delegations now silently no-op rather than raising.

`can_read()` reads the CPython-private `StreamReader._buffer` (same in `_AsyncRESPBase.can_read`). The comment says this will "fail loudly if the private buffer API changes", but the failure mode is a bare `AttributeError`, and `asyncio` `AbstractConnection.can_read()` only converts `OSError` into `ConnectionError` — so it would surface as an unexpected exception during pool checkout instead of a transport error. Consider a guarded read (e.g. capability check at import/connect time, or `getattr(self._stream, "_buffer", None)` with an explicit `RedisError`) so the failure is diagnosable and typed.

`_socket_can_read()` uses `select.select()`, which in CPython is limited by `FD_SETSIZE` (1024 on Linux/macOS): if the socket's file descriptor is >= 1024 it raises `ValueError: filedescriptor out of range in select()`. `_HiredisParser.can_read()` is on the hot path (`ConnectionPool.get_connection()` calls `connection.can_read()` for every acquisition, and PubSub polls it), and `Connection.can_read()` only translates `OSError`, so this `ValueError` escapes to callers. The previous recv-based probe had no such fd limit. Prefer `selectors.PollSelector`/`select.poll` (falling back to `select` only where poll is unavailable).

`AsyncBaseParser.can_read_destructive` is marked `@abstractmethod` while simultaneously being deprecated. Because `deprecated_function` wraps with `functools.wraps` (which copies `__dict__`, including `__isabstractmethod__`), the method stays abstract, so a third-party async parser that follows the PR's migration guidance and implements only `can_read()` will fail to instantiate with `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class ... with abstract method can_read_destructive`. Give the deprecated method a concrete default implementation (`return await self.can_read()`) instead of making it abstract.

`BaseParser.on_connect`/`on_disconnect` were converted from concrete methods raising `NotImplementedError` to `@abstractmethod`. Combined with the two new abstract methods on `AsyncBaseParser`, any existing third-party parser subclass that relied on inheriting these stubs can no longer be instantiated (TypeError at construction rather than at call time). This is an unrelated breaking change for a PR about readiness checks; consider leaving them concrete.

`can_read()` (here and in `_AsyncHiredisParser.can_read`) reads the private `asyncio.StreamReader._buffer`. Besides being an undocumented attribute, an `AttributeError` from an alternative/mocked stream object is not translated by `AbstractConnection.can_read()` (which only catches `OSError`), so it would surface as a raw `AttributeError` to callers instead of a `ConnectionError`. Consider guarding with `getattr(self._stream, "_buffer", b"")` or wrapping the access.

The signature rewrite switches to PEP 604 unions (`str | None`, `float | None`, `Mapping[int, int | bytes] | object | None`, `List["ssl.VerifyFlags"] | None`, ...) in annotations that are evaluated at *runtime*. Neither this file nor redis/asyncio/client.py, redis/asyncio/cluster.py or redis/asyncio/connection.py has `from __future__ import annotations` (evidenced by the fact that TYPE_CHECKING-only names still had to be quoted, e.g. `ssl_cert_reqs: "str | ssl.VerifyMode"`). On Python 3.9 — still a supported version per README ("redis-py 6.2.0 supports Python 3.9+") — `str | None` and `typing.List[...] | None` raise `TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for |` at import time, so `import redis` fails outright. Either add the future import to every touched module or keep `Optional`/`Union`. Additionally, `driver_info: DriverInfo | object | None` was previously written as `Union[Optional["DriverInfo"], object]`; if `DriverInfo` is only imported under `TYPE_CHECKING` in these modules, un-quoting it is a NameError on all Python versions.

Defaulting `socket_timeout` to 5s silently breaks every operation that intentionally blocks longer than the socket read timeout: `BLPOP/BRPOP/BLMOVE/XREAD BLOCK 0` (redis-py does not extend the socket timeout for blocking commands), `WAIT`, `Monitor`, and `PubSub.listen()`/`get_message(timeout=None)` (which call `read_response()` with the connection's socket timeout). With the default `retry_on_timeout=False`, these now raise `TimeoutError` after 5 idle seconds instead of blocking — including the PubSub example in the README. Either exempt the blocking paths (pass an explicit per-command timeout / disable the socket timeout for blocking commands and pubsub reads) or don't set a global default read timeout.

Enabling `socket_keepalive=True` plus a non-empty default `socket_keepalive_options` makes the per-option `setsockopt` loop in `Connection._connect()` run for every connection, on every platform. Two consequences: (1) the async `_connect` applies the option keys with `socket.SOL_TCP`, which is a Linux/glibc-only constant — on macOS/BSD (where `get_default_socket_keepalive_options()` returns `{socket.TCP_KEEPALIVE: 30, ...}`) the attribute lookup raises `AttributeError`, which is not covered by the surrounding `except (OSError, TypeError)` guard, so every async connect fails; (2) in the sync path an `OSError` from `setsockopt` is normalized into `ConnectionError`, so a platform/container that exposes a constant but rejects the option now fails to connect where it previously succeeded. Best-effort application of the *default* options (wrap in try/except per option, and use `IPPROTO_TCP` consistently) is needed before turning them on by default.

Lowering the default connection cap from 2**31 to 100 turns previously working high-concurrency workloads into hard failures, because neither `ClusterNode.acquire_connection` (async cluster) nor `ConnectionPool.get_connection` queues on exhaustion — they raise `MaxConnectionsError` immediately. The diff itself demonstrates the regression: `tests/test_asyncio/test_cluster.py::test_can_run_concurrent_pipelines` had to be changed to build the client with `max_connections=1000` to keep passing. Please either keep the cap unbounded by default, or make exhaustion block/wait (BlockingConnectionPool-like semantics) so existing applications degrade in latency instead of erroring.

Changing the default `socket_timeout` from `None` to 5s silently breaks every long-lived blocking read that redis-py performs with the socket timeout: `PubSub.parse_response(block=True)` (i.e. `listen()` / `get_message(timeout=None)`) uses `read_timeout = SENTINEL` → the connection's socket timeout, so an idle subscriber now raises `TimeoutError` every 5s and churns through reconnect/resubscribe until the retry budget is exhausted; the same applies to `Monitor.listen()` and to server-side blocking commands (`BLPOP`/`BRPOP`/`BLMOVE`/`XREAD BLOCK`/`WAIT`) whose timeout exceeds 5s. There is no blocking-command-aware timeout override in the client, so callers that never set `socket_timeout` will regress. Either exempt blocking reads (derive the socket timeout from the command's block timeout) or keep the read timeout unbounded by default.

Combining the new finite default `socket_timeout` (5s) with the default retry policy (`retries=10`, and `TimeoutError` is part of `Retry`'s default `supported_errors`) makes silent duplicate execution of non-idempotent commands the default behaviour: when the server executed a command but the client timed out, `_close_connection()` disconnects and `call_with_retry` re-sends the same command up to 10 more times (e.g. `INCR`, `LPUSH`, `XADD`, `RPOPLPUSH`). Previously `socket_timeout=None` made timeout-driven retries practically unreachable, so this is a new hazard for dependents. Consider not retrying on `TimeoutError` after the command was written, or documenting/limiting this prominently.

Lowering `ClusterNode.max_connections` (and `RedisCluster.max_connections`) from 2**31 to 100 is a hard failure mode for the async cluster client: `ClusterNode.acquire_connection()` raises `MaxConnectionsError` immediately when the per-node limit is reached (there is no waiting/blocking pool for cluster nodes), so previously working high-concurrency workloads now fail with an exception instead of queueing. The diff itself shows the regression: `tests/test_asyncio/test_cluster.py::test_can_run_concurrent_pipelines` had to be changed to build a client with `max_connections=1000` to keep passing. Either give the node pool blocking/wait semantics or pick a limit that does not turn concurrency into errors, and call this out as a breaking change.

The new docstrings for `Connection.__init__` (here and in `redis/asyncio/connection.py`) use NumPy-style `Parameters\n----------` sections, while CONTRIBUTING states the preferred docstring style for new code is Google style (as used by the `Args:` blocks added to `Redis.__init__` in this same PR).

`AsyncMaintNotificationsConnectionHandler.handle_maintenance_start_notification` never records the start-notification id (no `add_maint_start_notification`), and `handle_maintenance_completed_notification` never consults `get_processed_start_notifications()` / `add_skipped_end_notification()`. The sync handler in redis/maint_notifications.py does both (see the comment there: "handle the case when we receive more than one start notification before the final end notification"), and the new async connection mixin still exposes `add_maint_start_notification`, `get_processed_start_notifications`, `add_skipped_end_notification`, `get_skipped_end_notifications` — all dead code in the async path. As a result an END notification whose START was never seen (or an END for one maintenance window while another is still active, e.g. FAILED_OVER arriving while MIGRATING is in progress) immediately restores the original socket timeouts and sets state back to NONE, dropping the relaxed timeout while maintenance is still ongoing.

If `pool.apply_moving_notification(...)` raises, `handle_node_moving_notification` propagates the exception before `self._schedule(notification.ttl, self.handle_node_moved_notification, ...)` and before `self._processed_notifications.add(notification)`. This is reachable: `AsyncMaintNotificationsAbstractConnectionPool._disconnect_connections` gathers with `return_exceptions=True` and then re-raises the first exception, and async `AbstractConnection.disconnect()` can raise (e.g. TimeoutError while closing the writer). Because connection state has already been switched to MOVING (relaxed timeouts + new host) and `disconnect()` deliberately does not revert MOVING state (only MAINTENANCE), the pool and its connections are left permanently in MOVING with no TTL cleanup scheduled, and the exception also escapes into the caller's `read_response`. Failures while disconnecting free connections should be logged and swallowed (and the cleanup scheduling should be in a `finally`). Note also that re-raising a gathered `asyncio.CancelledError` in a non-cancelled task is undesirable.

In the `unix_socket_path` branch the kwargs are seeded with `"maint_notifications_config": MaintNotificationsConfig(enabled=False)`, but a few lines later `if maint_notifications_config: kwargs.update({"maint_notifications_config": maint_notifications_config})` runs unconditionally for both branches and overwrites it with the caller's config (e.g. `enabled="auto"`), so the explicit disable is dead code. Relatedly, the RESP3 check that follows also fires for Unix-socket clients (`Redis(unix_socket_path=..., protocol=2, maint_notifications_config=MaintNotificationsConfig(enabled="auto"))` raises "only supported with RESP version 3" even though maintenance notifications are unsupported on Unix sockets anyway). Move the enable/protocol handling into the TCP branch or drop the dead override.

`AsyncMaintNotificationsAbstractConnectionPool.update_maint_notifications_config` validates connection-class/host/path support but, unlike `__init__`, never checks the negotiated protocol. Calling it on a `protocol=2` pool installs an `AsyncMaintNotificationsPoolHandler` and writes `maint_notifications_config`/`maint_notifications_pool_handler` into `connection_kwargs`; the failure then surfaces late and inconsistently — existing connections raise `RedisError("Maintenance notifications are only supported with hiredis and RESP3 parsers!")` from `set_maint_notifications_pool_handler_for_connection`, and for an empty pool every subsequently created connection raises from `_configure_maintenance_notifications`, leaving the pool unusable. Add the same `check_protocol_version(..., 3)` guard used in `__init__`.

`set_maint_notifications_pool_handler_for_connection()` installs the parser handlers and the connection handler, but never initializes `orig_host_address` / `orig_socket_timeout` / `orig_socket_connect_timeout`. Those attributes are only assigned inside `_configure_maintenance_notifications()`, which returns early when the connection was constructed with notifications disabled. So after `await pool.update_maint_notifications_config(MaintNotificationsConfig(enabled=True))` (the documented "enable later" path, exercised by test_async_pool_update_config_wires_existing_connections), the pre-existing connection objects are reused with handlers attached but without those attributes. The first MIGRATED/FAILED_OVER notification (`handle_maintenance_completed_notification` -> `reset_tmp_settings`), the MOVING TTL cleanup (`reset_tmp_settings` via `update_connection_settings`), or `disconnect()` while in MAINTENANCE state will then raise `AttributeError` from inside the push-notification handler, i.e. inside the in-flight command's `read_response()`. Initialize the orig_* fields unconditionally in `AsyncMaintNotificationsAbstractConnection.__init__` (or in `set_maint_notifications_pool_handler_for_connection`).

`ConnectionPool.release()` now holds the pool-wide `self._lock` across `await connection.disconnect()`. `get_connection()` also acquires `self._lock`, so every release of a connection marked for reconnect stalls all connection acquisition for the duration of the socket teardown (up to `socket_connect_timeout`, which during maintenance has been relaxed to `config.relaxed_timeout`). This is exactly the hot path after a MOVING notification, where every in-use connection is marked for reconnect, so the reconnect storm gets serialized behind the pool lock. The lock is not needed for the disconnect: the connection has already been removed from `_in_use_connections` and is not yet in `_available_connections`, so no other task can obtain it. Move `await connection.disconnect()` outside the `async with self._lock` block (or use `nowait=True`).

`handle_node_moving_notification()` does not guard `await self.pool.apply_moving_notification(...)`. If it raises (e.g. `_disconnect_connections()` re-raises a `TimeoutError` from `connection.disconnect()`, or `_reschedule_active_read_timeout()` raises `RuntimeError`), the already-applied MOVING state (relaxed timeouts + rewritten host on matching connections) is never reverted because neither the TTL cleanup task is scheduled nor is the notification recorded in `_processed_notifications` — a retry of the same notification would also be treated as new. The exception additionally escapes the push-notification handler into the unrelated in-flight command's `read_response()`. Wrap the pool mutation so failures are logged and the TTL cleanup is still scheduled.

In `_reschedule_active_read_timeout()`, the `async-timeout` fallback path (Python < 3.11.3) calls `timeout_context.reject()` when the new timeout is `None` (i.e. `MaintNotificationsConfig(relaxed_timeout=None)`, documented as "blocking"). `async_timeout.Timeout.reject()` drops the timeout handler, and a later `update(deadline)` on the same context — which happens when the matching MIGRATED/FAILED_OVER notification calls `update_current_socket_timeout(-1)` during the same read — raises `RuntimeError("cannot reschedule timeout after reject()")`. That RuntimeError propagates out of the push handler and fails the in-flight command. Guard the reschedule (e.g. try/except RuntimeError) or track that the deadline was rejected.

`get_resolved_ip()` falls back to the blocking `socket.getaddrinfo()` call. This runs on the event loop (it is reachable from `MaintNotificationsConfig.get_endpoint_type()` during the connection handshake and from the debug logging helper), so a slow DNS server would block all other tasks. Consider `loop.getaddrinfo()` or dropping the fallback, since the peername lookup already covers the connected case.

`MaintNotificationsConnectionHandler._NOTIFICATION_TYPES` is now dead code: `handle_notification()` was switched to the module-level `_get_maintenance_notification_type()`. Remove the class attribute to avoid two sources of truth for the start/end classification.

The new OSS branch in `update_maint_notifications_config` installs `oss_cluster_maint_notifications_handler` (and writes it into `connection_kwargs`) without any of the guards that `__init__` applies for the same feature: no `check_protocol_version(..., 3)`, no `_maintenance_notifications_supported()` / connection-class / `path` check. A pool created with protocol 2 (or a custom connection class) can therefore be switched into OSS mode successfully, and the failure is deferred to per-connection setup (`_get_push_notifications_parser()` / `_configure_maintenance_notifications` raising `RedisError`), leaving the pool unusable and behaving differently for already-created vs future connections. Apply the same guards here as in `__init__`.

`set_maint_notifications_cluster_handler_for_connection` wires the OSS handler but never clears `self._maint_notifications_pool_handler` nor the parser's `node_moving_push_handler_func`. The surrounding comments in this diff assert OSS and pool-handler mode are mutually exclusive and that the switch clears the pool handler "so new and existing connections are not configured with both handlers", and the pool/kwargs paths do clear it — but existing connections (both the free and the in-use loops in `_update_maint_notifications_configs_for_connections`) keep the stale pool handler wired. The new test only asserts the absence of the pool handler on the pool and on a *newly created* connection, so the gap is untested. Either clear the pool handler here or drop the mutual-exclusion claim from the comments.

`aclose()` snapshots `handler._background_tasks` once, cancels and gathers that snapshot, then closes the nodes manager. `handle_oss_maintenance_completed_notification` itself schedules further tasks into `_background_tasks` (the `disconnect_free_connections()` tasks), so a task that is running/being cancelled can add children after the snapshot was taken; those are never cancelled or awaited and will run against a nodes manager that is being closed (pending-task warnings, or operations on closed connections). The tests' own `_drain_maint_notification_tasks` helper loops precisely because the handler spawns further tasks — `aclose()` should loop until the set is empty (or the handler should expose a cancel-all that does).

In `test_smigrating_smigrated_on_the_same_node_two_slot_ranges`, the assertion for "second migration still in progress -> timeout remains relaxed" uses `ConnectionStateExpectation(NODE_PORT_1)` (defaults: `changed_connections_count=0`, `state=MaintenanceState.NONE`, `relaxed_timeout=None`). In `_validate_connections_states` the predicate is `(state != NONE and state == expected.state) or (socket_timeout != None and socket_timeout == expected.relaxed_timeout)`, which can never be true for those defaults, so the count is always 0 and the check passes whether or not the timeout was relaxed. The final block (`changed_connections_count=0`, defaults) is vacuous for the same reason. Assert the relaxed state/timeout explicitly (e.g. expect count 1 with `state=MAINTENANCE`), and assert restoration by checking `socket_timeout`/`maintenance_state` directly.

`get_resolved_ip()` now returns `self.host` verbatim, so for an FQDN host it returns a hostname rather than a resolved IP — the method name/contract and the sync twin (which still resolves via `getaddrinfo`) now disagree.
