Avoiding blocking DNS on the event loop is right, but consider renaming/documenting the async method (or resolving via `loop.getaddrinfo` from an async helper) and verify no caller other than debug logging compares this value against an address.

Changing `rsplit("-", 1)[0]` to `rsplit("-", 2)[0]` in the shared `generate_params` helper strips an extra dash-separated segment from every scenario DB name, including the existing sync standalone scenarios that also use this helper. That can truncate names to a shorter, potentially colliding pattern (e.g. two suites resolving to the same db name). If only the new OSS-cluster configs need the extra suffix stripped, scope the change to those configs rather than changing the shared helper.

`AsyncOSSMaintNotificationsHandler.get_handler_for_connection()` is never called: `_configure_maintenance_notifications` and `set_maint_notifications_cluster_handler_for_connection` both wire the shared handler instance directly. It is a verbatim, awaitless copy of the sync helper; either use it (as the docstring implies each connection should get its own copy) or drop it, since dead helpers here usually mean a code path was not ported.

`_setup_cluster` is an async generator fixture but is declared with plain `@pytest.fixture`. This suite runs pytest-asyncio in strict mode (tests carry explicit `@pytest.mark.asyncio`, and the other async fixture added in this PR — `setup_and_cleanup` in tests/test_asyncio/test_scenario/test_maint_notifications.py — uses `@pytest_asyncio.fixture`). In strict mode a plain `@pytest.fixture` async generator is never awaited, so `self.proxy_helper`, `self.config` and `self.cluster` are never assigned and no teardown runs, making every test in `TestAsyncClusterMaintNotificationsHandling` error out (and leaking the proxy interceptors). Use `@pytest_asyncio.fixture(autouse=True)`.

The rewritten comment claims "Marking both in-use and free connections for reconnect lets them be lazily disconnected on next acquire", but this hunk changes comments only — the code below is untouched and (per the comment it replaces, and per the PR description) marks only the preserved node's *free* connections. The new comment, and the scenario-test comments that cite it ("set_nodes marks ALL preserved nodes' in-use connections"), will mislead the next reader. Either align the comment with the code or make the code do what the comment says.

`get_resolved_ip()` now returns `self.host`, which may be an FQDN rather than an IP, so the method no longer honours its name/contract and diverges from the sync implementation (which still resolves via `getaddrinfo`). Avoiding blocking DNS on the event loop is right, but consider renaming the accessor (or resolving via `loop.getaddrinfo` in an async helper) so sync/async debug output and any consumer expecting an address literal stay consistent.

Changing `rsplit("-", 1)[0]` to `rsplit("-", 2)[0]` alters the derived db-name pattern for every caller of `generate_params`, including the pre-existing sync scenario tests. For db config names that carry only one trailing segment this now strips one segment too many, silently changing the created database name. If only the new OSS-cluster-API configs need two segments stripped, gate the change on that path.

Dead code left from the sync-test port: `_preserve_startup_nodes_order` is a no-op that is never called, `_validate_removed_node_connections` is never used, and `NODE_IP_LOCALHOST` / `DEFAULT_SOCKET_TIMEOUT` are unused constants. Suggest removing them.

`AsyncMaintNotificationsConnectionHandler.handle_maintenance_completed_notification` does not port the sync handler's overlapping-window bookkeeping. The start path records ids via `add_maint_start_notification`, but the completion path unconditionally calls `reset_tmp_settings(reset_relaxed_timeout=True)` / `update_current_socket_timeout(-1)` / sets state to NONE without ever consulting `get_processed_start_notifications()` or calling `add_skipped_end_notification()`. Consequently an END notification whose START was never observed on this connection, or an END for one window (e.g. FAILED_OVER) while another (MIGRATING) is still active, prematurely drops the relaxed timeouts. The tell-tale sign is that `get_processed_start_notifications`, `add_skipped_end_notification` and `get_skipped_end_notifications` — all newly added to `AsyncMaintNotificationsAbstractConnection` — have no caller anywhere in the async code.

`AsyncMaintNotificationsAbstractConnectionPool.update_maint_notifications_config` does not apply the guards that `__init__` applies. It never calls `check_protocol_version(protocol, 3)`, and the `oss_cluster_maint_notifications_handler` branch also skips `_maintenance_notifications_supported()` / path / connection-class validation entirely. A RESP2 pool (or a pool with an unsupported connection class) can therefore be switched into maintenance-notification mode: `_update_connection_kwargs_for_maint_notifications` writes the handler into `connection_kwargs`, and then `_update_maint_notifications_configs_for_connections` raises `RedisError` from `_get_push_notifications_parser()` partway through the loop, leaving the pool half-configured (kwargs updated, some connections wired, others not) and behaving differently for existing vs. future connections. Mirror the constructor validation before mutating any state.

The `MaintNotificationsConfig(enabled=False)` seeded inside the `unix_socket_path` branch is dead: the later unconditional `if maint_notifications_config: kwargs.update({"maint_notifications_config": maint_notifications_config})` overwrites it with the caller's config. Worse, the RESP3 validation above it is not scoped to the TCP branch, so a Unix-socket client constructed with `protocol=2` and `MaintNotificationsConfig(enabled="auto")` raises "Maintenance notifications handlers on connection are only supported with RESP version 3" for a feature that can never apply to Unix sockets. Scope both the kwargs handling and the protocol check to the TCP branch.

`test_smigrating_smigrated_on_the_same_node_two_slot_ranges` is deleted, removing the only regression test for the overlapping-maintenance-window behaviour ("the timeouts are not unrelaxed if a second migration is in progress") on the sync side, at the same time as the async port omits that bookkeeping entirely. Either adapt the test to the new `_validate_connections_states` semantics or add an equivalent async test, otherwise a premature un-relaxation of timeouts during overlapping SMIGRATING/SMIGRATED windows will go undetected.

`set_maint_notifications_pool_handler_for_connection()` / `set_maint_notifications_cluster_handler_for_connection()` wire the parser handlers and the connection-level handler onto an *existing* connection, but never initialize the `orig_host_address` / `orig_socket_timeout` / `orig_socket_connect_timeout` snapshot (only `_configure_maintenance_notifications()`, which runs in `__init__`, does that). These are exactly the paths taken by `ConnectionPool.update_maint_notifications_config()` for connections created while maintenance notifications were disabled. The first "maintenance completed" notification on such a connection calls `reset_tmp_settings(reset_relaxed_timeout=True)`, and the new reset block in `disconnect()` does the same, both of which read `self.orig_socket_timeout` -> `AttributeError` inside a push-notification handler. Please snapshot the orig_* values (if unset) when enabling handling on an existing connection.

`BlockingConnectionPool.get_connection()` only serializes on `self._lock` while `_in_maintenance` is set, and that flag is only toggled by `apply_moving_notification()`. The delayed `run_proactive_reconnect()` (used when a MOVING notification carries no new host) and `cleanup_moving_notification()` mutate pool state under `_lock` without setting the flag, so for BlockingConnectionPool they can interleave with `get_connection()`. Concretely, `_run_proactive_reconnect_without_locking()` collects the free connections and then awaits `_disconnect_connections()`; during that await a concurrent `get_connection()` (flag == False, so no lock) can pop one of those still-listed connections from `_available_connections` and `connect()` it, only for the in-flight `disconnect()` to tear it down again — the caller gets a dead connection. Either set/clear the maintenance flag around these two operations as well, or always take the pool lock in `BlockingConnectionPool.get_connection()`.

`ensure_connection()` now skips the "Connection has data" / "Connection not ready" guard whenever maintenance notifications are enabled — which is the default for RESP3 pools after this change. That silently disables the long-standing detection of a desynchronized connection (one returned to the pool with an unread command response), so a leftover reply can be mis-read as the next command's response. Consider draining the pending frames instead (e.g. `read_response(push_request=True)` while data is buffered, as `process_invalidation_messages()` does) so genuine leftover *command* data is still detected.

`MaintNotificationsConnectionHandler._NOTIFICATION_TYPES` is no longer read now that `handle_notification()` uses the new module-level `_get_maintenance_notification_type()` helper. Leaving it in place creates a second, divergent source of truth for the start/completed notification classes (and vulture, which runs in `invoke linters`, is likely to flag it). Please delete it.

`def get(self, name: str) -> HImportFieldset | None:` uses a PEP 604 union in an unquoted annotation, and this new module has no `from __future__ import annotations`. Function annotations are evaluated at definition time, so on Python 3.9 (still supported per README) this raises `TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for |: 'type' and 'NoneType'` at import — and because `redis/_parsers/response_callbacks.py` now imports `redis.himport`, plain `import redis` fails outright on 3.9. Either add the future import to this module or use `Optional[HImportFieldset]`.

New parameter annotated `himport_registry: HImportRegistry | None = None` in `AbstractConnection.__init__` (same pattern added to `NodesManager.__init__` in redis/cluster.py). Both signatures are evaluated at import time and the neighbouring params in these very signatures still use `Optional[...]`, indicating no `from __future__ import annotations` in these modules — on Python 3.9 the PEP 604 union raises TypeError at import. Use `Optional[HImportRegistry]` (as the surrounding code does) unless the future import is present/added.

This `str = None` -> `str | None = None` sweep is unrelated to the HIMPORT feature and carries real risk: `redis/exceptions.py` is imported by everything, and if it lacks `from __future__ import annotations` these PEP 604 unions in `__init__` signatures break `import redis` on Python 3.9 (still supported). Please drop the cosmetic churn from this PR, or use `Optional[str]`.

`himport_registry` is injected unconditionally into `connection_kwargs` (same in redis/asyncio/connection.py). `connection_class` is a documented extension point, so every third-party/custom connection class with an explicit keyword signature (and libraries such as fakeredis) will now fail with `TypeError: __init__() got an unexpected keyword argument 'himport_registry'` merely by upgrading — a silent breaking change for a feature the user never opted into. Note the sync cluster path already demonstrates the non-breaking alternative (`create_redis_node` assigns `pool.himport_registry` after construction); consider keeping the registry on the pool only and attaching it to connections after `make_connection()`, or injecting the kwarg lazily. As a side effect, `pool.connection_kwargs` equality assertions now break (only the async test file was updated; check tests/test_connection_pool.py).

The new per-node HIMPORT pre-flight loop is inserted after the node connections have been checked out of their pools but (judging by the surrounding comments/`start_time` placement) before the `try:`/`finally:` block that releases `n.connection` back to `n.connection_pool`. `prepare_pipeline` can raise (ResponseError from a bad PREPARE, ConnectionError on write), which would leak every connection acquired for this batch. Move the loop inside the try whose finally releases the connections.

`pipeline_prepares` (and its async twin) only short-circuits on `isinstance(registry, HImportRegistry)`, but a registry now always exists on every pool/connection, so the guard never fires. Every pipeline/transaction execution for every user therefore scans all buffered commands through `parse_himport_set_args` — a real per-command cost on a hot path for users who never touch HIMPORT. Add a cheap empty-registry short-circuit (e.g. `if registry.revision == 0: return []` or `if not len(registry) ...`) before the scan and before `reconcile_discards`.

The new command docstrings (`himport_prepare_internal`, `himport_set`, `himport_discard_internal`, `himport_discard_all_internal`) omit the house-style trailer used by neighbouring commands: an 'Available since Redis X.Y' line plus 'For more information, see https://redis.io/commands/<command>'. This matters more than usual here because the commands need a preview server (and the PR itself is inconsistent about whether that is 8.9 or 8.10).

The test gate is `skip_if_server_version_lt("8.9.0")` (both this file and the async mirror), while the README text added in this PR and the CI image bump say the feature requires Redis 8.10. If HIMPORT only exists in 8.10, running the suite against an 8.9 server produces hard 'unknown command' failures instead of skips. Align the gate with the actual introducing version.

Public docstring reads "Each call to current command returns a *new* client" in both `master_for` and `slave_for`, while the sync twin says "Each call to the current method" / "Each call to current method". All four are grammatically broken and drifted between the sync/async twins; name the method explicitly (e.g. "Each call to ``master_for`` returns a *new* client...") and keep the wording identical in redis/sentinel.py.

`class TestIsHImportSetCommand` is decorated with `@pytest.mark.fixed_client` twice (duplicated line). Also note the import block puts `from redis._parsers.base import BaseParser` after `from redis.connection import ...`; `invoke linters` (isort/ruff-I) will flag that here and in tests/test_asyncio/test_multidb/test_pipeline.py, where `from redis.exceptions import DataError` was inserted between two `redis.asyncio.multidb` imports.

`himport_prepare`/`himport_discard`/`himport_discard_all` are defined on `Redis` and reference `self._single_connection_client`, but `Pipeline` (which subclasses `Redis` and never calls `Redis.__init__`) does not set that attribute — so `pipe.himport_prepare(...)` raises `AttributeError`. The async mirror is worse: `redis/asyncio/client.py::himport_prepare` starts with `await self.initialize()`, and `Redis.initialize()` reads `self.single_connection_client`, which the async `Pipeline` also never sets. This is exactly the flow the new README section recommends (`with r.pipeline(transaction=False) as pipe: pipe.himport_prepare(...)`), and no test exercises `pipe.himport_prepare` — only `client.himport_prepare` followed by pipelined `himport_set`. Either override these on the Pipeline classes (they are registry-only, so they cannot be queued anyway and returning `True` instead of the pipe also breaks chaining/`execute()` result arity), or guard the attribute access and fix the README example.

`himport_registry` is injected unconditionally into `connection_kwargs` (same in `redis/asyncio/connection.py`), so it is now passed to every `connection_class` constructor. Any user-supplied `connection_class` that does not accept `**kwargs` (a supported extension point) will start raising `TypeError` on first connection creation, and `pool.connection_kwargs` — an observable public dict that consumers compare/copy — gains an internal object (hence the `OMIT_REPR_KEYS` workaround and the relaxed assertions in tests/test_asyncio/test_connection_pool.py; note the sync `tests/test_connection_pool.py` equality assertions are not updated here). Consider keeping the registry on the pool only and having the HIMPORT executors resolve it from the pool/client rather than threading it through `connection_kwargs`.

The HIMPORT note added to `slave_for` is copy-pasted from `master_for` and is misleading: it tells users the returned client "exposes the HIMPORT command family" and then states "(`himport_set` is a write and is served by the master.)" — but a `slave_for` client connects to a replica, so `himport_set` will fail with a READONLY error, not be routed to the master. Also the sentence "Each call to current method returns a *new* client" is garbled in both `slave_for` docstrings (sync and `redis/asyncio/sentinel.py`).

The new module uses `@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)` for `CommandMetadata` (the `slots=` argument only exists from Python 3.10) and PEP 604 unions in annotations that are evaluated at runtime (`request_policy: RequestPolicy | None = ...` in the dataclass body, `-> CommandMetadata | None`, `fallback: MetadataResolver | None = None`, `dict[str, CommandPolicies | None]`) without `from __future__ import annotations`. This module is on the plain `import redis` path (redis/cache.py -> redis/commands/metadata.py), so if the declared minimum interpreter is still 3.9 (README claims 3.9+), importing the package fails outright with `TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for |` / `TypeError: dataclass() got an unexpected keyword argument 'slots'`. Note the surrounding new code is inconsistent about this: the `ConnectionPool`/`RedisCluster` parameters added in the same PR use `Optional[MetadataResolver]`. Please either confirm the floor is >=3.10 or use `Optional[...]` and drop `slots=True`.

The live-server drift guards for the shipped table are gated on `STATIC_TABLE_SERVER_VERSION = "8.10.0"`, but the comment inside `test_the_live_chain_broadens_eligibility_only_through_its_fallback` states the counts were "Measured against the pinned redislabs/client-libs-test stack image (Redis 8.9.241)". If CI still pins that image, every test in `TestStaticMetadataAgainstServer` and its async mirror is skipped, so the new `_STATIC_COMMAND_METADATA` table — the thing this PR makes authoritative for both routing and cache eligibility — has no executed validation against a real `COMMAND` reply. The same test also hard-codes `assert len(eligible - allow_list) == 53`, which is tied to that specific module image and will fail (or silently stay skipped) on any image bump. Related nit: the sync docstring says "servers before 8.9" for the `script_runner` flag while the async mirror says "before 8.10".

Deprecation versions introduced in the same change disagree: `STATIC_POLICIES` warns with `version="8.1.0"` while `CommandsParser.get_command_policies` / `AsyncCommandsParser.get_command_policies` warn with `version="8.2.0"`. Since both surfaces are deprecated by this PR, pick one release string so the deprecation timeline reported to users is consistent.

`_to_command_policies` withholds routing policies only when they are `None`, so any policy a metadata record carries is passed through verbatim to the cluster client. Since `RedisCluster` now derives its `policy_resolver` from a caller-supplied `metadata_resolver`, a resolver built from a live `COMMAND` reply will hand the client `RequestPolicy.MULTI_SHARD` for common commands (DEL, UNLINK, MSET, MSETNX, TOUCH, and EXISTS/MGET wherever the static table does not shadow them). The comments in this very file state that MULTI_SHARD "is not implemented in either client stack" and that "recording the real tips here therefore breaks the command" - which is exactly why the static table substitutes the keyed defaults. That makes the documented server-driven configuration (`metadata_resolver=StaticMetadataResolver(fallback=DynamicMetadataResolver(records))` on a cluster client, which `docs/resp3_features.rst` presents without the caveat) break DEL/UNLINK/MSET at execution time; only the `RedisCluster` docstring warns, and the mitigation is to pass a second argument. Consider having the projection (or the client) withhold policies the client cannot honour, so a metadata-derived routing resolver degrades to client-side slot resolution instead of reaching the unimplemented path.

`STATIC_TABLE_SERVER_VERSION = "8.10.0"` gates the whole `TestStaticMetadataAgainstServer` drift guard (and its async mirror), but a comment inside `test_the_live_chain_broadens_eligibility_only_through_its_fallback` in the same class states the pinned `redislabs/client-libs-test` stack image is Redis 8.9.241. If that is the image CI runs, every `@skip_if_server_version_lt(STATIC_TABLE_SERVER_VERSION)` test - i.e. the entire guarantee that `_STATIC_COMMAND_METADATA` still matches a real `COMMAND` reply - is skipped and never executed. Either the gate or the pinned image needs to move; otherwise the hand-maintained table has no working drift protection.

`test_the_live_chain_broadens_eligibility_only_through_its_fallback` asserts `len(eligible - allow_list) == 53`, a hard-coded count derived from the server's and every loaded module's command metadata. Any stack image bump (new module command, new readonly command, changed tip) fails this test with no indication of what actually regressed, and the failure is unrelated to this client's behaviour. The two structural assertions above it (nothing dropped beyond the three server-confirmed defects; every newly eligible command comes from the fallback layer) already carry the guarantee; consider dropping the exact count or asserting the diff set explicitly so a failure is self-describing.

`CacheConfig.DEFAULT_ALLOW_LIST` remains a public class attribute but is now never read. Editing/extending it was the only supported way to change client-side-cache eligibility before this change (e.g. `CacheConfig.DEFAULT_ALLOW_LIST.append("MYCMD")` or subclassing with a narrower list), and such code now silently stops having any effect - no warning, no error, just commands that quietly stop being cached or start being cached. Consider emitting a deprecation warning when the attribute is accessed (as `redis.commands.policies.STATIC_POLICIES` does via module `__getattr__`), or honouring a subclass-overridden list, so the behaviour change is discoverable at runtime rather than only in a source comment.

The rationale comment above `_MEMO_MAX_ENTRIES` justifies the cap by saying "the default resolver a client gets is a single instance evaluated at import and shared by every client in the process". This PR deliberately changes that: `Redis`, `RedisCluster`, `ClusterPipeline` and `CacheConfig` each build their own resolver, and the new tests (`test_the_default_resolver_is_built_per_client`, `test_the_default_metadata_resolver_is_built_per_client`) assert precisely that no such process-wide instance exists. The comment should be updated so the stated reason for the cap matches the design.
